title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: Alexey Alexandrovitch had forgotten Countess Lidia Ivanovna, but she had not forgotten him. At the worst point of his lonely despair she came to him, and without waiting to be announced she walked straight into his study. She found him sitting with his head in both hands.

"_J'ai forcé la consigne_," she said, sweeping in with quick steps, breathing hard from excitement and the speed of her walk. "I have heard everything! Alexey Alexandrovitch! Dear friend!" she went on, warmly squeezing his hand in both of hers and gazing into his eyes with her fine, pensive ones.
Frowning, Alexey Alexandrovitch stood up, eased his hand free, and pulled a chair over for her.
"Won't you sit down, countess? I'm not receiving anyone — I'm unwell, countess," he said, and his lips twitched.

"Dear friend!" Countess Lidia Ivanovna repeated, not taking her eyes off his. Suddenly her eyebrows rose at the inner corners, making a triangle on her forehead; her plain yellow face grew plainer still — but Alexey Alexandrovitch could feel that she was sorry for him and on the verge of tears. He softened too; he grabbed her plump hand and started kissing it.
"Dear friend!" she said in a voice that cracked with feeling. "You must not give in to grief. Your sorrow is great, but you have to find consolation."

"I am crushed, I am annihilated, I am no longer a man!" said Alexey Alexandrovitch, letting go of her hand but still gazing into her brimming eyes. "My position is so terrible because I can find no support anywhere — not even inside myself."

"You will find support. Seek it — not in me, though I beg you to believe in my friendship," she said with a sigh. "Our support is love, the love He has granted us. His burden is light," she said, with that look of ecstasy Alexey Alexandrovitch knew well. "He will be your support and your help."

Although there was in these words a touch of that self-congratulatory emotion at her own elevated feelings, and of that new mystical fervor which had recently spread in Petersburg and which Alexey Alexandrovitch found overblown, it was still pleasant to him to hear it now.
"I am weak. I am crushed. I foresaw none of this, and now I understand none of it."
"Dear friend," Lidia Ivanovna repeated.

"It's not the loss of what I no longer have — it isn't that!" Alexey Alexandrovitch went on. "I don't grieve for that. But I cannot help feeling humiliated in front of other people for the position I'm in. It's wrong, but I can't help it, I can't help it."

"That noble act of forgiveness was not performed by you — it was done through you. I was moved to ecstasy by it, and so was everyone else. He was working inside your heart," said Countess Lidia Ivanovna, lifting her eyes rapturously, "and so you cannot be ashamed of what you did."
Alexey Alexandrovitch knit his brows and, bending his fingers back, cracked his knuckles.

"One has to know all the facts," he said in his thin voice. "A man's strength has its limits, countess, and I have reached mine. The whole day I have been having to make arrangements — household arrangements arising" (he stressed the word _arising_) "from my new, solitary position. The servants, the governess, the accounts.... These pinpricks have stabbed me to the heart, and I do not have the strength to bear it. At dinner ... yesterday, I was almost ready to get up from the table. I could not stand the way my son looked at me. He did not ask what any of it meant, but he wanted to, and I could not bear the look in his eyes. He was afraid to look at me, but that is not all...." Alexey Alexandrovitch would have mentioned the bill that had been brought to him, but his voice shook and he stopped. He could not think of that bill on blue paper, for a hat and ribbons, without a wave of self-pity.

"I understand, dear friend," said Lidia Ivanovna. "I understand all of it. Help and comfort you will not find in me, though I have come precisely in order to help if I can. If only I could lift these petty, humiliating cares off you.... I understand that a woman's word, a woman's supervision is needed. Will you entrust it to me?"
Silently and gratefully Alexey Alexandrovitch pressed her hand.
"Together we will look after Seryozha. Practical matters are not my strong suit. But I will get to work. I will be your housekeeper. Don't thank me. I am not doing it on my own account...."
"I cannot help thanking you."

"But, dear friend, do not give in to that feeling you spoke of — being ashamed of what is the Christian's highest glory: _he who humbles himself shall be exalted_. And you cannot thank me. You must thank Him, and pray to Him for help. In Him alone we find peace, consolation, salvation, and love," she said, and turning her eyes upward, she began to pray, as Alexey Alexandrovitch gathered from her silence.

Alexey Alexandrovitch listened to her now, and the phrases that had earlier seemed to him, if not actually distasteful, at least overdone, now sounded natural and consoling. He had disliked this new enthusiastic strain of religion. He was a believer who was interested in religion mainly for its political aspect, and the new doctrine, which dared to offer several new interpretations — precisely because it opened the door to debate and analysis — was on principle disagreeable to him. He had until now taken a cold, even hostile, attitude toward this new teaching, and with Countess Lidia Ivanovna, who had been swept up by it, he had never argued, but had carefully fended off her attempts to draw him into argument by saying nothing. Now for the first time he listened to her words with pleasure, and inwardly did not push back against them.
"I am very, very grateful to you, both for what you have done and for what you have said," he said when she had finished praying.
Countess Lidia Ivanovna once more pressed both her friend's hands.
"Now I will start my duties," she said with a smile after a pause, as she wiped away the traces of tears. "I'm going to Seryozha. I'll only come to you as a last resort." And she got up and went out.
Countess Lidia Ivanovna went into Seryozha's part of the house and, letting tears fall on the frightened child's cheeks, told him that his father was a saint and his mother was dead.

Countess Lidia Ivanovna kept her promise. She really did take on the organization and running of Alexey Alexandrovitch's household. But she had not been exaggerating when she said practical matters were not her strong suit. Every arrangement she made had to be modified because it couldn't be carried out, and the modifications were made by Korney, Alexey Alexandrovitch's valet, who — without anyone realizing it — now actually ran Karenin's household and quietly, discreetly, reported to his master while dressing him on everything Karenin needed to know. But Lidia Ivanovna's help was real all the same: she gave Alexey Alexandrovitch moral support through her conscious love and respect for him, and — what was even more soothing for her to believe — she almost converted him to Christianity. That is, from an indifferent and listless believer she turned him into a fervent and committed adherent of the new interpretation of Christian doctrine that had lately been gaining ground in Petersburg. It was easy for Alexey Alexandrovitch to believe in this teaching. He, like Lidia Ivanovna and the others who shared their views, was entirely without vividness of imagination — that spiritual faculty by which the images called up by the imagination become so real that they have to be brought into line with other ideas and with actual facts. He saw nothing impossible or unthinkable in the idea that death, while it existed for unbelievers, did not exist for him; that since he possessed the most perfect faith — and he himself was the judge of how perfect it was — there was therefore no sin in his soul, and he was already experiencing complete salvation here on earth.

It is true that the falseness and shallowness of this conception of his faith were dimly available to Alexey Alexandrovitch himself, and he knew that back when he had given way to the feeling of forgiveness with no idea at all that his forgiveness was the act of a higher power, he had felt more happiness than he did now, when at every moment he was thinking that Christ was in his heart and that, in signing official papers, he was carrying out His will. But for Alexey Alexandrovitch it was a necessity to think in that way. It was such a necessity for him, in his humiliation, to have some elevated vantage point, however imaginary, from which — though he was looked down on by everyone — he could look down on others, that he clung, as to his sole salvation, to his illusion of salvation.
